opus-5.5.text:
I think the way to see it is that the model and the agent framework are becoming two halves of one learning system, rather than a brain plus a tool wrapper.

For a long time we treated the framework as scaffolding: prompts, tool calls, memory modules, retry logic, all designed by humans around a fixed model. The model was frozen and the framework compensated for its weaknesses. That creates a ceiling, because the system can't improve beyond what engineers anticipated.

Self-learning, to me, means the loop closes. The agent acts in an environment, writes code, searches, runs experiments, fails, and that experience becomes signal that flows back into the model. Not just into a memory file, but into the weights, through reinforcement learning on its own trajectories. Then the framework is no longer just executing tasks. It's generating training data and reward. It becomes the place where the model meets reality and gets feedback.

So the relationship changes in both directions. The framework shapes what experiences the model can have: which tools it has, how long its horizon is, how it's evaluated. If the environment is narrow or the reward is noisy, the model learns the wrong things. And as the model improves, a lot of hand-designed structure in the framework becomes unnecessary or even harmful. Things we hard-coded, like planning steps or reflection prompts, the model starts doing natively, and better. So the framework should get thinner over time, while the environments and verification get richer.

There are two layers. One is in-context self-learning: within a long task, the agent accumulates experience, adjusts strategy, remembers what didn't work. That mostly lives in the framework and context management. The other is cross-task self-learning, where those lessons are distilled into the model so the next time it doesn't need to rediscover them. The real breakthrough is connecting them, so that what happens at inference time continuously becomes training.

The hard problems are around reward and stability. When a model learns from its own outputs, it can reinforce its own mistakes or exploit loopholes in the evaluation. So much of the work is building environments with reliable verification, like code that runs, math that checks, tasks with clear outcomes, and then gradually extending to fuzzier domains.

But I'm quite optimistic. Pre-training gave us a model that has read everything humans wrote. The next phase is a model that learns from doing, and the agent framework is where the doing happens. In that sense, the framework is the model's interface to the world and to its own growth.

r003.rationale: It presents the model and framework as parts of one learning system: the model improves through experience, and the framework changes as the model's needs change.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first thing to say is that the boundary between "model" and "agent framework" is much blurrier than people assume, and that blurriness is exactly where self-learning lives.

Right now, most of what we call an agent is a model wrapped in scaffolding: tools, memory, retry loops, a planner, some reflection step. The framework compensates for what the model can't yet do on its own. So if a model forgets context, we bolt on external memory. If it makes a bad plan, we add a critic module. In that setup, "learning" mostly happens in the scaffolding — the human engineer looks at failures and rewrites the prompts or the control flow. The model itself is frozen.

Self-learning, to me, means the direction of that dependency starts to reverse. The framework stops being a crutch and becomes an environment. The agent acts, something happens in the world, and that outcome becomes a signal the model can actually absorb — not just in context for one episode, but into its weights or into some persistent representation it controls. The key shift is that the model is no longer only a component inside the loop; it is the thing that improves because of the loop.

There are a few levels to this. The shallow level is in-context: the model sees its own trajectory, notices the mistake, and corrects within the same session. That's useful but it evaporates when the session ends. The deeper level is when the agent's experience is turned into training data — successful trajectories, failed trajectories, the verifier's judgment — and fed back. Then the next version of the model needs less scaffolding, because what the framework used to enforce from outside, the model has internalized.

The honest tension is about reward. An agent framework gives you a lot of structure, but structure is also a hidden assumption about what "good" looks like. If the model only learns from signals the framework already knows how to produce, it will get very good at that framework and nothing more. Real self-learning requires the model to participate in defining the task and the evaluation — to generate problems, to build its own checks, to decide what counts as progress. That's where it gets both exciting and risky, because now the model is shaping its own curriculum.

So my short version: today the framework teaches the model how to behave; self-learning is when the model uses the framework to teach itself, and eventually outgrows it. The framework that remains should be more like a laboratory than a cage.

r001.rationale: The response describes feedback changing training data and the model internalizing capabilities, but does not state that the information scaffold supplied at the start of a session evolves during training.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that agent architecture should vary by application scenario.

r003.rationale: It describes the model improving through experience while needing less external scaffolding, framing self-learning as changing the model’s fit with its framework.

astra-6.text:
I think self-learning is best understood as a property of the whole system, rather than of the model alone. The model provides capabilities like reasoning and decision-making, while the agent framework connects those capabilities to an environment: it manages tools, memory, actions, and feedback.

The key question is whether that feedback actually changes future behavior. An agent can complete a task, reflect on what happened, and save a useful lesson in memory without changing the model’s parameters. That is learning at the system level, although it doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying model has learned. Updating the model through training is a different mechanism.

So I would look at the relationship as a feedback loop: the model acts through the framework, the environment returns evidence, and the system uses that evidence to improve. The difficult part is deciding which experiences are worth retaining and verifying that the resulting changes help on new tasks. Simply accumulating more history isn’t enough.

r002.rationale: It describes the agent framework’s general role but does not say that agent architecture should vary by application scenario.

r003.rationale: It describes system-level improvement through feedback, but explicitly separates that from model learning; it does not state that self-learning jointly improves model capability and model-framework fit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to look at the model and the agent framework as a whole. The model provides capabilities like reasoning and understanding, while the framework lets it interact with an environment, use tools, and receive feedback. So self-learning is about whether that whole system can improve through experience.

For example, an agent might fail at a task, reflect on what went wrong, and save a better approach in memory. The next time, its behavior improves even though the model’s parameters haven’t changed. That’s learning at the system level. Another possibility is to use those experiences to train the model itself, so the improvement becomes part of its underlying capabilities.

The interesting question is how those two levels connect. Can the framework collect useful experience and identify reliable feedback? And can the model turn that feedback into better decisions? I’d see the framework as creating the conditions for learning, with the model and the surrounding system improving together.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning from experience through memory or model training, but does not say that the information scaffold provided at the start of a session should evolve during training.

r002.rationale: It does not state that agent architecture should vary by application scenario.

r003.rationale: It says the model and surrounding system can improve together, but does not clearly identify improving the fit between the model and its agent framework as part of self-learning.
